claim: Dictyostelium discoideum is an obligatory aerobic organism that requires at least 5% O2 to grow at optimal exponential rate.
source: Dd is an obligatory aerobic organism that requires at least 5% O2 to grow at optimal exponential rate (Cotter and Raper, 1968; Sandonà et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Cotter and Raper, 1968; Sandonà et al., 1995).

claim: Dictyostelium discoideum can grow at slower rates at 2% O2.
source: while slower growth can occur at 2% O2
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Sandonà et al., 1995) mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: High oxygen level is one of the signals used to trigger culmination of the migrating slug in Dictyostelium discoideum.
source: During its multicellular motile stage, high oxygen level is one of the signal used to trigger culmination of the migrating slug (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Xu et al., 2012).

claim: When a Dictyostelium discoideum cell colony is covered, cells quickly consume the available oxygen and form a dense ring moving outwards at constant speed and density.
source: When a cell colony is covered, cells quickly consume the available oxygen (O2) and form a dense ring moving outwards at constant speed and density.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript, including Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: The formation time of the dense ring depends non-linearly on initial cell density, with denser colonies forming rings faster.
source: This formation time however depended non-linearly on initial cell density (the denser, the faster, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The collective migration of the dense ring can be self-maintained for tens of hours, even days, and the ring can span centimeters.
source: Once triggered, this collective migration was self-maintained for tens of hours, even days and the ring could, at these points, span centimeters (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The vertical confinement between the bottom of the plate and the coverslip is 50 μm.
source: We measured the vertical confinement through confocal microscopy and found the height between the bottom of the plate and the coverslip to be 50 μm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: As the ring expands outwards, it leaves a trail of cells behind that do not contribute directly to the migration of the ring.
source: Notably, as the ring expanded outwards, it left a trail of cells behind. This led to the formation of a central zone populated by cells which did not contribute directly to the migration of the ring (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cells behind the ring in the hypoxic region have an elongated phenotype resembling pre-aggregative Dictyostelium discoideum cells.
source: This led to the formation of a central zone populated by cells which did not contribute directly to the migration of the ring (Figure 1B) but were still alive and moving albeit a clear elongated phenotype resembling pre-aggregative Dd cells (Figure 1C and Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C and Video 2.

claim: Cells in the ring or outside the colony are rounder, as usual vegetative cells.
source: In comparison, cells in the ring or outside the colony were rounder, as usual vegetative cells (Delanoë-Ayari et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and comparison to prior research (Delanoë-Ayari et al., 2008).

claim: After a transitory period, the density in the ring, its width, and its speed all remain constant over long time scales.
source: We found that after a transitory period corresponding to the ring passing through the initial spot, the density in the ring, its width and its speed all remained constant over long time scales (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The speed of the ring is 1.2 ± 0.3 μm/min (mean ± std, N=9 independent experiments).
source: The speed and density of the ring were found to be 1.2 ± 0.3 μm/min (mean ± std, N=9 independent experiments)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from 9 independent experiments.

claim: The density of the ring is 1.9 103 ± 0.3 103 cells/mm2 (mean ± std, N=4 independent experiments), which is fourfold higher than behind it.
source: and 1.9 103 ± 0.3 103 cells/mm2 (mean ± std, N=4 independent experiments, that is fourfold higher than behind it, Figure 1E) respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from 4 independent experiments and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The density of cells left behind the ring remains constant after a transient regime.
source: The density of cells left behind the ring was also found to remain constant after a transient regime (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The absence of changes in ring morphology over time implies an increase in the number of cells and thus an important role of cell division.
source: As the diameter of the ring increased over time, the absence of changes in morphology implies an increase of the number of cells and thus an important role of cell division.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the observation that the ring expands while maintaining constant density and width.

claim: Cell diffusion constant and instantaneous cell speeds are fairly constant throughout the entire colony.
source: Both the cell diffusion constant and instantaneous cell speeds were fairly constant throughout the entire colony (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cell diffusion is 28.2 ± 1.4 μm2/min (N=3 independent experiments, each containing at least 2000 cells).
source: Cell diffusion was 28.2 ± 1.4 μm2/min (N=3 independent experiments, each containing at least 2000 cells)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from 3 independent experiments.

claim: Significantly non-zero biases in cell motion are observed only in a region spanning the entire ring and a few tens of microns behind and in front of it, with the strongest positive biases found in the ring.
source: Here, we found that significantly non-zero biases were observed only in a region spanning the entire ring and a few tens of microns behind and in front of it with the strongest positive biases found in the ring (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Behind the ring in the hypoxic region, cells have elongated shape, normal speeds, and low bias.
source: Overall, our results show that the different regions defined by the ring and its dynamics can be characterized in terms of cell behavior: (i) behind the ring in the hypoxic region: elongated shape, normal speeds, and low bias;
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: In the ring, cells have round shape, normal speeds, and high bias.
source: (ii) in the ring: round shape, normal speeds and high bias.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Dictyostelium discoideum cells exhibit aerotactic and aerokinetic response in a low range of O2 concentration.
source: We showed that Dictyostelium cells exhibit aerotactic and aerokinetic response in a low range of O2 concentration indicative of a very efficient detection mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations in microfluidic devices described in the manuscript.

claim: Dictyostelium discoideum cells show an aerokinetic positive response to low oxygen, even in the absence of gradients.
source: The very significant difference (p<0.0001) demonstrates that Dd cells show an aerokinetic positive response to low oxygen, even in the absence of gradients.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements comparing cell motility at different homogeneous oxygen concentrations.

claim: Cell diffusion constant at 0.4% O2 is D=40.2±9.6 µm2/min (mean ± std).
source: We found cell diffusion constant to be D=40.2±9.6 µm2/min (mean ± std) at 0.4% (Figure 2—figure supplement 8)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Cell diffusion constant at atmospheric oxygen concentrations (20.95%) is D=19.2±8.8 µm2/min.
source: At atmospheric oxygen concentrations though, this effective diffusion was clearly reduced as we measured it to be D=19.2±8.8 µm2/min (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Cells accumulate at a similar O2 concentration of about 1% in all three microfluidic channels with different gaps.
source: However, our O2 sensors indicated that the accumulation occurred at a similar O2 concentration of about 1% in all three channels (inset of Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements using O2 sensors shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The parameter controlling the aerotactic response is O2 levels.
source: thus strongly hinting that the parameter controlling the aerotactic response was O2 levels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that cell accumulation occurs at similar O2 concentrations across different gradient conditions.

claim: The aerotactic bias measured in microfluidic experiments is 1.1 ± 0.4 µm/min (N=6, three independent experiments and for each, both directions of the gradient).
source: We measured the bias for the different gaps and for the situation of reversed gradient and obtained a value of 1.1 ± 0.4 µm/min (N=6, three independent experiments and for each, both directions of the gradient, each value stemming from a few hundred cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from 6 conditions across 3 independent experiments.

claim: The position of the ring closely follows the dynamics of the O2 field.
source: At this point, coupled dynamics between the cells and the O2 distribution appeared and we observed that the position of the ring closely followed the dynamics of the O2 field (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ring follows a constant concentration of oxygen of 0.25%.
source: that is it followed a constant concentration of oxygen of 0.25% (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Behind the ring, O2 is completely depleted and thus no gradient is visible.
source: Behind the ring, O2 was completely depleted and thus no gradient was visible.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of O2 distribution in the spot assay.

claim: In front of the ring, the O2 concentration remains high with high gradients.
source: In front of the ring, the O2 concentration remained high with high gradients.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of O2 distribution in the spot assay.

claim: In the ring region, O2 is low (<1%) and the gradients are strong.
source: Finally, in the ring region, O2 was low (<1%) and the gradients were strong.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of O2 distribution in the spot assay.

claim: The cellular Potts model reproduces the results of microfluidic experiments qualitatively and quantitatively in terms of collective behavior, cell accumulation, and individual cell behavior.
source: Through a trial and error procedure, we managed to reproduce these results qualitatively and quantitatively (Video 4) in terms of collective behavior, cell accumulation, and individual cell behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Video 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cellular Potts model shows the rapid formation and migration of a ring similar to that observed in experiments.
source: We then applied this model and added O2 consumption by cells, with initial conditions mimicking our spot assay and other ingredients mimicking the vertical confinement. We observed the rapid formation and migration of a ring (Figure 4A–B, Video 5). This ring was remarkably similar to that observed in experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4A-B and Video 5.

claim: The speed of the simulated ring is constant after an initial transitory period and comparable to experimental speeds.
source: In particular, we found its speed to be constant after an initial transitory period (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). This speed was also comparable to experimental ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The morphology of simulated rings is constant over time with a fixed cell density and width.
source: Similarly, the morphology of these simulated rings was constant over time with a fixed cell density and width (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the cellular Potts model, the ring follows a constant O2 concentration.
source: In terms of coupled dynamics between cell density and O2 profiles, we found here too that the driving force behind this collective phenomenon was the fact that the ring followed a constant O2 concentration (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Dividing cell consumption of oxygen by a factor of 3 does not significantly change the ring speed but can change the aspect of cell density in the central region.
source: We started by dividing cell consumption of oxygen by a factor of 3 (Figure 5A) and found that it did not significantly change the ring speed but could change the aspect of cell density in the central region.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Turning off cell division in the cellular Potts model leads to the ring starting to slow down and eventually stopping after a short time.
source: If we turned off cell division in our models, the formation of the ring was mostly unchanged but after a short time, the ring started slowing down and even stopped as cell density was no longer sufficient to reach highly hypoxic conditions (comparing Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Aerokinesis is not necessary to reproduce the collective migration in the cellular Potts model.
source: Second, we asked whether the observed and modeled aerokinesis was necessary to reproduce the collective migration. We found that it wasn't as models ran at different effective temperatures applied to all cells regardless of local O2 concentrations all showed qualitatively similar behavior (see for example Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Lower effective temperatures in the cellular Potts model lead to less dense rings as fewer cells are able to start in the ring.
source: Of note though, lower effective temperatures led to less dense rings as fewer cells were able to start in the ring (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Modulation of aerotaxis by local O2 concentrations is essential for forming a dense ring in the cellular Potts model.
source: Finally, we found that modulation of aerotaxis by local O2 concentrations was essential. Indeed, as we increased the range of O2 concentration at which aerotaxis is at play (Figure 5G–H), we found that forming rings became wider and less dense (Figure 5D–E) to the point where no actual ring could be distinguished if aerotaxis was kept constant for all cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5D-I.

claim: Cell division and aerotactic modulation are the two key ingredients to reproduce the ring of cells in the cellular Potts model.
source: These numerical simulations based on cellular Potts models provide a good intuition of the phenomenon and reveal that cell division and aerotactic modulation are the two key ingredients to reproduce the ring of cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results exploring different model variations.

claim: When Dictyostelium discoideum cells are placed in phosphate buffer medium lacking nutrients, a ring of cells starts forming and expanding outwards at short time scales, but after a few hours the ring starts slowing down until it completely stops.
source: In this situation, at short time scales, a ring of cells started forming and expanding outwards in a similar fashion as in nutritive medium (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). After a few hours, however, the ring started slowing down until it completely stopped and cells started dispersing again.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The experimental result of placing cells in phosphate buffer is in complete agreement with the predictions of the Cellular Potts Model.
source: This is in complete agreement with the predictions of the Cellular Potts Model, as one can see by comparing the density kymographs (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and firmly demonstrates the importance of cell division in this behavior.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison between experimental results and computational model predictions.

claim: At longer time scales (t>10h) in phosphate buffer, Dictyostelium discoideum cells start forming aggregates and entering a developmental phase.
source: At longer time scales though (t>10h), Dd cells started forming aggregates and entering a developmental phase (Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Video 6.

claim: The aggregation in phosphate buffer is presumably due to the concomitant expression of cell adhesion molecules and apparition of self-organizing secreted cAMP pulses.
source: This aggregation is presumably due to the concomitant expression of cell adhesion molecules and, apparition of self-organizing secreted cAMP pulses whose timing agrees with the one reported in classical free cell spot aggregation assays (Gregor et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by comparison to prior research (Gregor et al., 2010).

claim: When two colonies are simulated in close proximity, the formed rings rush toward one another and fuse together to make an elliptical front which then relaxes towards a more circular shape.
source: We started exploring this question by simulating two colonies put in close proximity. These simulations predict that the formed rings do not repel each other, instead they tend to rush toward one another and, when they meet, they fuse together to make an elliptical front which then relaxes towards a more circular shape (Video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Video 7.

claim: The experimental behavior of two colonies in close proximity is very similar to the simulation predictions.
source: We then performed the corresponding experiment and found very similar behavior (Video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Video 7.

claim: The cellular Potts model recapitulates all the major experimental observations with only two key ingredients: cell division and aerotactic modulation.
source: Overall, these results show that the cellular Potts model indeed recapitulates all the major experimental observations with only two key ingredients (cell division and aerotactic modulation).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the computational modeling results and their comparison to experiments.

claim: In the case of large bias, the wave undergoes a spatially uniform mixing of two colored populations.
source: In the case of large bias (Figure 7A–C), the wave is pushed and the profile is a perfect mixture of blue and yellow cells at long times.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: In the case of small bias, the wave is pulled and only cells that were initially in the front are conserved in the front.
source: Contrarily, the wave is pulled in the regime of small bias: only cells that were already initially in the front, here colored in blue (Figure 7B–D), are conserved in the front, whilst yellow cells at the back cannot catch up with the front.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: The cellular Potts model with neutral labeling shows clear, rapid mixing of two cell populations under the propagation of a pushed wave.
source: In the absence of associated experimental data, we explored the cellular Potts model with such neutral labeling. The results were in agreement with the PDE simulations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) showing a clear, rapid mixing of the two cell populations under the propagation of a pushed wave in the regime of experimental parameter values.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The propagation speed of the 'Go or Grow' model with a second threshold remains close to the value given by the formula for the elementary model (at most 15% relative difference in a relevant range of parameters).
source: In the general case, we were not able to do a thorough analysis of this model, but through numerical exploration we found that the propagation speed remained close to the value given by formula (Equation 6) (at most 15% of relative difference in a relevant range of parameters, Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A wide combination of aerotaxis and cell division can drive the propagation of a stable wave with various density profiles.
source: This numerical exploration indicates that a wide combination of the two key ingredients, aerotaxis and cell division, can drive the propagation of a stable wave with various density profiles.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from computational modeling results exploring different model variations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oxygen can play the role of the attractant in self-generated gradients.
source: Finally, our work goes beyond theses results as it demonstrates that oxygen can play the role of the attractant in self-generated gradients therefore potentially extending the physiological relevance of the use of such cues in collective migration.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fact that the dense front of cells follows a constant oxygen concentration provides a hint that any situation in which cell density is locally high enough to trigger hypoxic conditions will also lead to a similar behavior.
source: The fact that the dense front of cells follows a constant oxygen concentration (Figure 3E, Figure 4E) provides a hint that any situation in which cell density is locally high enough to trigger hypoxic conditions will also lead to a similar behavior.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental and modeling observations shown in Figure 3E and Figure 4E.

claim: In three dimensions, if oxygen is provided on all sides, a spherical front of cells starts moving outwards in the cellular Potts model.
source: Briefly, we show that in three dimensions, if oxygen is provided on all sides, a spherical front of cells starts moving outwards (Video 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D computational modeling results shown in Video 8.

claim: In three dimensions, if the bottom of the space is completely deprived of oxygen, the front migrates upwards only in a half-spherical shape in the cellular Potts model.
source: However, if we assumed that the bottom of the space was completely deprived of oxygen (i.e. a symmetry breaking situation that can be encountered in various physiological situations), this front was migrating upwards only in a half-spherical shape (Video 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D computational modeling results shown in Video 8.

claim: The key to proper steering in self-generated oxygen gradients are high enough cell densities and the creation of robust self-generated gradients.
source: Our 2d results can therefore be extended to any other situations and they show that the key to proper steering are high enough cell densities and the creation of robust self-generated gradients.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dictyostelium discoideum cells exhibit an aerokinetic and aerotactic response within 15 min when exposed to externally imposed O2 gradients.
source: Within 15 min, cells exhibit an aerokinetic and aerotactic response when exposed to externally imposed O2 gradients (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Self-generated O2 gradients are produced within 20 min in the spot assay.
source: Self-generated O2 gradients are produced within 20 min (Figure 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cellular response of Dictyostelium discoideum is within the equilibration time of the oxygen distribution, so the cellular response can be considered as almost instantaneous.
source: But this cellular response is within the equilibration time of the oxygen distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 6). Hence we can consider the cellular response as almost instantaneous with Dd.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The difference in response time between Dictyostelium discoideum and previously studied cells is probably due to the extreme plasticity of the rapidly moving amoeboid cells and their almost adhesion independent migration mechanism.
source: The difference with previously studied cells is probably due to the extreme plasticity of the rapidly moving amoeboid cells (Dd) and their almost adhesion independent migration mechanism (Friedl et al., 2001) while mesenchymal cancer cells move slower by coordinating cytoskeleton forces and focal adhesion (Palecek et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by comparison to prior research (Friedl et al., 2001; Palecek et al., 1997).

claim: The molecular mechanisms used for O2 sensing and its transduction into cellular response in Dictyostelium discoideum are for the moment unknown.
source: The molecular mechanisms used for O2 sensing and its transduction into cellular response are for the moment unknown
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the current state of research.

claim: The O2 molecular sensors in Dictyostelium discoideum may modulate cytoskeleton organization, particularly localized actin polymerization/depolymerization through some of the molecular components involved in classical chemotaxis toward folate or cAMP.
source: but we can expect that the O2 molecular sensors modulate cytoskeleton organization, particularly localized actin polymerization/depolymerization through some of the molecular components involved in classical chemotaxis toward folate or cAMP (Pan et al., 2016; van Haastert et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by comparison to prior research (Pan et al., 2016; van Haastert et al., 2017).

claim: The self-generated LPA and folate gradients were modeled with a simple numerical model that was able to predict the steady wave.
source: The self-generated LPA (melanoma) and folate (Dd) gradients were modeled with a simple numerical model that was able to predict the steady wave.
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior research on self-generated gradients in other systems.

claim: The model of self-generated gradients predicted an invasive front where cells are exposed to a steep chemoattractant gradient, followed by a 'trailing end' where the gradient is shallow and fewer cells migrate with poor directionality.
source: In particular, it predicted an invasive front where cells are exposed to a steep chemoattractant gradient, followed by a 'trailing end' where the gradient is shallow and fewer cells migrate with poor directionality (Tweedy and Insall, 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior research (Tweedy and Insall, 2020).

claim: The model of self-generated gradients predicted that the wave may have a less marked front, and/or a smaller speed, or even vanish if the cell density was too low due to insufficient chemoattractant removal.
source: It also predicted that the wave may have a less marked front, and/or a smaller speed, or even vanishes if the cell density was too low due to insufficient chemoattractant removal.
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior research on self-generated gradients.

claim: The features predicted by the model of self-generated gradients are surprisingly similar to the experimental measurements of cell density and O2 profiles in this study.
source: All these features are surprisingly similar to our experimental measurements of cell density and O2 profiles (Figure 1E, Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison between prior modeling work and experimental results from this study shown in Figure 1E and Figure 3C.

claim: The atmospheric O2 that diffuses through the culture medium and eventually the plastic surfaces is the chemoattractant in the spot assay.
source: The atmospheric O2 that diffuses through the culture medium and eventually the plastic surfaces is the chemoattractant.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental setup and observations.

claim: The O2 consumption triggers hypoxia that in turn generates an aerotactic response toward O2 in a very narrow range of O2 concentrations (0–1.5%).
source: The O2 consumption triggers hypoxia that in turn generate an aerotactic response toward O2 in a very narrow range of O2 concentrations (0–1.5%) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cell growth is necessary to produce a long-standing wave without any damping effect.
source: Cell growth is necessary to produce a long-standing wave without any damping effect.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling results.

claim: In the experiments under study, directional motion contributes the most to the cell speed, ruling out the possibility of seeing a pulled wave driven by cell division and diffusion at the edge of the front.
source: In the experiments under study, we estimate directional motion to contribute the most to the cell speed, ruling out the possibility of seeing a pulled wave driven by cell division and diffusion at the edge of the front.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling analysis applied to experimental parameter values.
